prerequisites: It is highly recommended that students have taken and passed "Mechanics and Thermodynamics", "Linear Algebra", and "Calculus" from the 1st semester of the 1st year.
Elementary vector calculus. Concept of derivative and integral, with application to elementary functions.
System of linear equations and matrices.
Elementary concepts of particle kinematics and dynamics. Concept of force and Newton's principles. Work, kinetic and potential energy, and energy conservation.
Kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies. Mass geometry. Moments of inertia.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity and critical reasoning.
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering, both orally and in writing, and to all types of audiences.
Ability to manage specifications, regulations and mandatory standards.
Ability to work in a team.
Understanding and mastery of basic concepts on the general laws of mechanics, thermodynamics, fields and waves, and electromagnetism and their application to solving problems typical of engineering.
Knowledge of the principles of theory of machines and mechanisms.
Analyze and kinematically synthesize mechanisms.
Formulate and solve the direct and inverse dynamic problem of a planar mechanism.
Analyze and design rigid and flexible transmissions.
Know widely used mechanisms and understand that many seemingly different mechanisms respond to the same kinematic principles.
Create kinematic diagrams of real mechanisms as a form of representation and understand the mechanism's operation from such a diagram.

Structurally analyze articulated mechanisms by criteria of nature and number of links or pairs, and by dimensional criteria, describing, as a result, the degrees of freedom or mobility of the mechanism and the existence or not of dead or return points and their singularities.
Know and develop the concepts, fundamentals, and methods applied to the kinematic and dynamic analysis of planar mechanisms.
Calculate velocities, accelerations, and forces in any planar mechanism, for specific positions of the mechanism and for complete movement cycles.
Determine the type and dimensions of a bar mechanism to perform a specific function (problem known as mechanism synthesis).
Assimilate the relationships between actions and the movement they produce in machines and be able to recognize the type of dynamic problem associated with each case.
Determine the inertia effects supported by the links or bars that make up the mechanisms.
Correctly include friction forces in sliding, rotating pairs, and rolling, and analyze and understand the operation of friction-based mechanisms.
Know and define the key dimensions and characteristics of motion transmissions between rotating shafts (gears, belts, ...).
Determine transmission ratios in ordinary and epicyclic gear trains and know the preferred design criteria used to define the number of teeth.
Describe the role played by cam mechanisms, pointing out their advantages and disadvantages in relation to other mechanisms that achieve the same results.
Use software for the analysis, simulation, and design of machines and mechanisms.
Analyze and select information from various sources.
Develop the ability to understand and interpret the results obtained through kinematic and dynamic analysis of mechanisms and machines.

syllabus_topics: Topic 1. Mechanisms and machines. Basic concepts and schematization.
Definition, general structure and components of a machine
Classification of kinematic elements and pairs
Mobility of mechanisms: Grübler and Kutzbach criteria
Four-bar linkage and kinematic inversion. Grashof's law
Topic 3. Analysis of velocities and accelerations.
Method of relative velocities and accelerations.
Direct dynamic analysis on reduced mechanisms
Flywheels: Steady state, degree of irregularity, concept of GD2
Friction in sliding, rotating pairs and rolling.
Concept of balancing. Balancing of mechanisms.
Topic 9. Introduction to rigid motion transmissions.
Fundamentals, terminology and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Topic 11. Helical cylindrical, bevel and worm gears.
Fundamentals, terminology and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Ordinary and epicyclic trains. Willis' formula.
Fundamental design law and kinematics of cams.
teaching_methods: Laboratory practices (software simulation, analysis, report writing)
Use of specific software for mechanism design and simulation
Visualization of real mechanical systems and prototypes
assessment_rules: For ordinary and June extraordinary calls, the final grade is calculated as Continuous Assessment (EC) + Lab Practices (PL) + Final Exam (EF). A minimum of 3 out of 7.5 points on the Final Exam (EF) is required to pass; otherwise, the final grade will be 4.9. EC and PL grades are retained for the June extraordinary call but not for previous years. For January extraordinary and differentiated evaluations, the assessment consists of a single written exam covering the course syllabus (90%) and laboratory content (10%). A minimum of 5 out of 10 points is required to pass this exam.
